item.title: Getting Started with Graph Neural Networks for Protein–Ligand Complexes Using DGL
item.description:
A fingerprint collapses a docked complex to a fixed vector. A graph keeps the atoms, the bonds, and the contacts, and a GNN learns from that neighborhood. is the PyTorch library this note uses. The code below is the path from an empty graph to a label. Readout and, for a set of poses, the bag come after message passing.

The rest is the DGL user-guide path, in the language of a protein–ligand complex. No prior GNN course is assumed.

Why Graphs for Molecules?

A molecule has a natural graph structure. Atoms are nodes, bonds are edges. When you extend this to a protein–ligand complex, you can add edges for non-covalent contacts (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, π-stacking) connecting ligand atoms to binding-pocket residues.

The key advantage: a GNN can aggregate information from a node’s neighborhood iteratively, so after a few layers, each atom’s representation encodes not just its own identity but the chemical context around it. This is exactly what a human medicinal chemist does mentally when reading a 2D structure.

The DGL Core: DGLGraph

Everything in DGL revolves around the DGLGraph object. Think of it as a PyTorch-native container for graph-structured data.

import dgl
import torch

# Define edges as (source_nodes, destination_nodes)
src = torch.tensor([0, 0, 1, 2])
dst = torch.tensor([1, 2, 2, 3])

g = dgl.graph((src, dst))
print(g)
# Graph(num_nodes=4, num_edges=4, ndata_schemes={}, edata_schemes={})

For molecular graphs, edges are usually undirected (bond A→B is the same as B→A), so use dgl.to_bidirected():

g = dgl.to_bidirected(g)

Attaching Features

Node and edge features are stored as PyTorch tensors directly on the graph:

# Node features: e.g., one-hot atomic number, partial charge, aromaticity...
g.ndata['feat'] = torch.randn(g.num_nodes(), 32)

# Edge features: e.g., bond type, interatomic distance...
g.edata['dist'] = torch.randn(g.num_edges(), 1)

This is the bridge between your cheminformatics featurization pipeline (RDKit, MDAnalysis, etc.) and the GNN. Whatever features you compute, just stick them in ndata or edata.

Heterogeneous Graphs: Protein + Ligand Together

If you want to model protein–ligand contacts explicitly (not just the ligand in isolation), DGL supports heterogeneous graphs: graphs with multiple node and edge types.

g = dgl.heterograph({
 ('ligand_atom', 'bond', 'ligand_atom'): (lig_src, lig_dst),
 ('ligand_atom', 'contacts', 'protein_residue'): (lig_ids, res_ids),
 ('protein_residue', 'contacts', 'ligand_atom'): (res_ids, lig_ids),
})

g.nodes['ligand_atom'].data['feat'] = ligand_atom_features
g.nodes['protein_residue'].data['feat'] = residue_features

This is a more faithful representation of the complex: the network can learn that certain binding-pocket residues modulate the ligand’s representation depending on how they interact.

Message Passing: How GNNs Actually Work

This is the heart of DGL and the heart of every GNN. Message passing works in two steps per layer:

Step 1: Edge-wise (messages): For each edge, compute a “message” from the source node’s features (and optionally the edge’s own features).

Step 2: Node-wise (aggregation + update): Each node collects all incoming messages, aggregates them (sum, mean, or max), and updates its own features.

Mathematically, for node v at layer t+1:

$$h_v^{(t+1)} = \psi\!\left(h_v^{(t)},\ \rho\!\left(\left\{ \phi(h_u^{(t)}, h_v^{(t)}, w_{uv}) : u \in \mathcal{N}(v) \right\}\right)\right)$$

where φ is the message function, ρ is the aggregation (e.g., mean), and ψ is the update function.

In DGL code, the fastest way uses built-in functions:

import dgl.function as fn

# Message: copy source node feature → edge mailbox
# Reduce: average all incoming messages → update node feature
g.update_all(fn.copy_u('h', 'm'), fn.mean('m', 'h'))

This runs as fused CUDA kernels, much faster than writing Python loops.

For custom behavior (e.g., distance-weighted messages):

def weighted_message(edges):
 # edges.src['h']: source node features
 # edges.data['dist']: edge distance
 return {'m': edges.src['h'] * torch.exp(-edges.data['dist'])}

g.update_all(weighted_message, fn.sum('m', 'h'))

Built-in GNN Layers

DGL ships with ready-to-use layers in dgl.nn.pytorch. The most useful for molecular tasks:

Layer When to use
GraphConv Simplest baseline, no edge features
GATConv Learns per-edge attention weights; great for contacts with varying importance
NNConv Edge-feature-conditioned messages; use when bond type or distance matters
HeteroGraphConv Wraps per-relation convolutions for heterogeneous graphs

A simple two-layer GAT:

import dgl.nn.pytorch as dglnn
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class MolGNN(nn.Module):
 def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden_dim):
 super().__init__()
 self.gat1 = dglnn.GATConv(in_dim, hidden_dim, num_heads=4)
 self.gat2 = dglnn.GATConv(hidden_dim * 4, hidden_dim, num_heads=1)

 def forward(self, g, feat):
 h = F.elu(self.gat1(g, feat).flatten(1)) # (N, hidden*4)
 h = self.gat2(g, h).squeeze(1) # (N, hidden)
 return h

Graph-Level Prediction: Readout

After message passing, each node has a learned embedding. For a graph-level prediction (e.g., is this compound active?), you need to compress the variable-number of node embeddings into a single fixed-size vector. This is called readout.

DGL provides built-in readout functions:

# Mean of all node features → one vector per graph
graph_embedding = dgl.mean_nodes(g, 'h')

# Also available: dgl.sum_nodes, dgl.max_nodes

For a batch of graphs (many compounds at once):

bg = dgl.batch([g1, g2, g3, ...]) # one disconnected super-graph
# ... run message passing on bg ...
embeddings = dgl.mean_nodes(bg, 'h') # shape (batch_size, hidden_dim)

dgl.batch() is what makes mini-batch training efficient: DGL treats the batch as a single large graph (with no edges between the individual molecules), runs all convolutions in one GPU call, then recovers per-graph embeddings with readout.

The Full Graph Classification Pipeline

Putting it all together: a classifier that takes a molecule graph and outputs a binary label:

import dgl
import dgl.nn.pytorch as dglnn
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class GraphClassifier(nn.Module):
 def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden_dim, n_classes=2):
 super().__init__()
 self.conv1 = dglnn.GATConv(in_dim, hidden_dim, num_heads=4)
 self.conv2 = dglnn.GATConv(hidden_dim * 4, hidden_dim, num_heads=1)
 self.classify = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, n_classes)

 def forward(self, g, feat):
 # Message passing
 h = F.elu(self.conv1(g, feat).flatten(1))
 h = self.conv2(g, h).squeeze(1)

 # Store updated features
 with g.local_scope():
 g.ndata['h'] = h
 # Readout: mean over all atoms → graph embedding
 graph_feat = dgl.mean_nodes(g, 'h')

 return self.classify(graph_feat)


# Training loop sketch
model = GraphClassifier(in_dim=32, hidden_dim=64)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

for epoch in range(100):
 for batched_graphs, labels in dataloader:
 feats = batched_graphs.ndata['feat']
 logits = model(batched_graphs, feats)
 loss = loss_fn(logits, labels)
 optimizer.zero_grad()
 loss.backward()
 optimizer.step()

Building a Dataset

DGL has a dataset API that handles caching processed graphs to disk, important when building graphs from PDB/SDF files is slow.

class MolDataset(dgl.data.DGLDataset):
 def __init__(self, raw_dir):
 super().__init__(name='mol_dataset', raw_dir=raw_dir)

 def process(self):
 self.graphs, self.labels = [], []
 for path in self._get_files():
 g, label = self._build_graph(path) # your featurization here
 self.graphs.append(g)
 self.labels.append(label)

 def __getitem__(self, i):
 return self.graphs[i], self.labels[i]

 def __len__(self):
 return len(self.graphs)

 def has_cache(self):
 return os.path.exists(self.save_path)

 def save(self):
 dgl.save_graphs(self.save_path, self.graphs,
 {'labels': torch.tensor(self.labels)})

 def load(self):
 self.graphs, label_dict = dgl.load_graphs(self.save_path)
 self.labels = label_dict['labels'].tolist()

Pair this with a DataLoader using dgl.dataloading.GraphDataLoader (or PyTorch’s standard DataLoader with a custom collate_fn that calls dgl.batch()).

Multiple Instances per Compound: the Bag Approach

A common scenario in ensemble docking: you dock one compound against N different receptor conformations and get N poses, each a separate graph. You want to make one prediction per compound, not one per pose.

This is a natural fit for Multiple Instance Learning (MIL). The trick with DGL:

def predict_bag(model, bag_of_graphs):
 # Stack all N pose-graphs into one batched graph
 bg = dgl.batch(bag_of_graphs)
 feats = bg.ndata['feat']

 # Run GNN - poses stay disconnected (no cross-pose edges)
 h = model.encode(bg, feats) # node embeddings

 with bg.local_scope():
 bg.ndata['h'] = h
 pose_embeds = dgl.mean_nodes(bg, 'h') # (N, h_dim) - one per pose

 # MIL aggregation over the bag
 bag_embed = pose_embeds.mean(0, keepdim=True) # mean pooling
 return model.classify(bag_embed)

The key insight: dgl.batch() keeps the poses structurally independent (no edges cross between them), so the GNN respects the fact that each pose is a separate physical structure. The MIL aggregation then decides how to combine them for the final prediction.

For a more expressive aggregation, use attention MIL:

class AttentionMIL(nn.Module):
 def __init__(self, h_dim):
 super().__init__()
 self.attention = nn.Sequential(
 nn.Linear(h_dim, 64),
 nn.Tanh(),
 nn.Linear(64, 1)
 )

 def forward(self, pose_embeds): # (N, h_dim)
 scores = self.attention(pose_embeds) # (N, 1)
 weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=0)
 return (weights * pose_embeds).sum(0) # (h_dim,)

Attention MIL has a nice bonus: weights tells you which poses contributed most to the prediction, interpretable by design.

Which Chapters to Read First

If you’re using this post as a reading guide alongside the :

Priority Chapter Why
⭐⭐⭐ Ch 1.2–1.5: Graphs, features, heterograph Core data structure
⭐⭐⭐ Ch 2.1–2.2: Message passing API The computation engine
⭐⭐⭐ Ch 5.4: Graph classification Your prediction task
⭐⭐ Ch 3: GNN modules Ready-to-use layers
⭐⭐ Ch 4: Data pipeline Dataset + caching
⭐ Ch 6–8: Stochastic / distributed / mixed precision Only if dataset is huge

Summary

DGL wraps the complexity of graph-structured computation behind a clean PyTorch API. For molecular applications, the workflow is:

  1. Build a DGLGraph for each complex: atoms as nodes, bonds/contacts as edges, features from your cheminformatics toolkit
  2. Choose a GNN layer: GATConv is a strong default
  3. Run message passing: each atom aggregates information from its neighbors
  4. Apply readout (dgl.mean_nodes) to get a fixed-size graph embedding
  5. Feed into a standard MLP classifier

The library handles batching, GPU transfer, and efficient sparse operations under the hood. Once you get the featurization right, the training code looks almost identical to a standard PyTorch image classifier.

item.title: Beyond 2D Fingerprints: Encoding Protein-Ligand Interactions for Machine Learning
item.description:
A 2D fingerprint throws away the pose. Docking spent its time on contacts, hydrogen-bond geometry, and stacking, and a topology-only vector keeps none of that. Use a 2D fingerprint when the ligand alone is the object. Use a 3D interaction fingerprint when the pose is the object.

PLEC, SPLIF, and E3FP are three different objects. PLEC encodes which groups touch. SPLIF encodes the geometry of those contacts. E3FP never sees the protein.

PLEC

PLEC is an ECFP-style fingerprint of the interface. It describes the chemical neighborhood of contacting atom pairs, on both the ligand and the protein. The model sees which groups are next to which residue environments, and at what depth you asked for.

Use it when the chemistry of the contact is the signal: affinity, or reactivity at a site.

import oddt
import oddt.fingerprints as fps
from oddt.toolkits.rdk import readfile

# Load receptor and ligand
receptor = next(readfile('pdb', 'receptor.pdb'))
receptor.protein = True

ligand = next(readfile('sdf', 'docked_pose.sdf'))

# Calculate PLEC fingerprint
# depth_ligand and depth_protein control circular environment depth
plec = fps.PLEC(ligand, receptor, depth_ligand=2, depth_protein=4, size=16384)

size is the bit length. A longer vector collides less and costs more memory. 16384 is the starting point given here for ensemble docking.

If the task is reactivity at one catalytic site, a hand-built distance can be appended. The coordinate below is a placeholder.

import numpy as np
from oddt.interactions import close_contacts

# Example: compute distance from ligand centroid to a metal/active site atom
# Replace with your actual active site coordinate
active_site_coord = np.array([12.3, 45.6, 7.8])
ligand_centroid = ligand.atoms.coords.mean(axis=0)
dist_to_site = np.linalg.norm(ligand_centroid - active_site_coord)

# Append to PLEC vector
plec_extended = np.append(plec, dist_to_site)

close_contacts is imported in the original snippet and not called. The distance is a centroid-to-point norm.

SPLIF

SPLIF encodes the geometry of interacting fragments rather than a catalog of atom types. Stacking and T-shaped contacts sit in that geometry, without a hard-coded interaction list. That makes it less tied to one docking program’s interaction labels.

Use it when you want poses that reproduce the 3D binding geometry of a reference ligand.

# SPLIF is also available through ODDT
splif = fps.SPLIF(ligand, receptor, depth_ligand=1, depth_protein=1, size=4096)

The vectors are sparser than PLEC. Tanimoto similarity on them is the geometric comparison in this note.

from oddt.utils import binary_tanimoto

reference_splif = fps.SPLIF(reference_ligand, receptor)
similarity = binary_tanimoto(splif, reference_splif)
print(f"Geometric similarity to reference: {similarity:.3f}")

E3FP

E3FP is a circular fingerprint in Euclidean space. It grows out from atoms through distance, not through bonds. The same 2D structure in two conformations gets two fingerprints. The protein is absent, so this is a ligand-shape method: ligand-based screening and scaffold hopping.

# Install e3fp: pip install e3fp
from e3fp.pipeline import fprints_from_mol
from rdkit import Chem
from rdkit.Chem import AllChem

# Load mol with a 3D conformer
mol = Chem.MolFromSmiles('your_smiles_here')
mol = Chem.AddHs(mol)
AllChem.EmbedMolecule(mol, AllChem.ETKDGv3())
AllChem.MMFFOptimizeMolecule(mol)

# Generate E3FP fingerprints for all conformers
fprints = fprints_from_mol(mol, fprint_params={'bits': 4096, 'level': 5})

# Convert to dense array for ML
import numpy as np
e3fp_array = np.array(fprints[0].to_vector(sparse=False), dtype=np.float32)

For several poses, this note mean-pools the vectors.

# Mean-pool across poses - preserves pharmacophoric signal while reducing noise
fprint_arrays = [np.array(fp.to_vector(sparse=False)) for fp in fprints]
e3fp_consensus = np.mean(fprint_arrays, axis=0)

Which one

PLEC SPLIF E3FP
Sees Protein and ligand Protein and ligand Ligand only
Encodes Contact chemistry Spatial geometry Shape and pharmacophore
Ensemble noise Tolerates it well Moderate Needs aggregation
Use Reactivity, affinity Geometric screening Ligand-based screening

Across an ensemble of receptor conformations, PLEC has a frame of reference the protein supplies, so the encoding moves less when the pose jitters. E3FP has to be aggregated or the conformer noise is the feature.

None of the three is complete. The pipelines this note describes do best when a primary fingerprint is joined to a few hand-built features that the fingerprint is not learning. Profile what the model uses before you swap the whole representation.

2D fingerprints stay the right tool for a fast ligand-only screen. For a model whose question is the binding geometry, the 3D choice above is the one that matches the question.

item.title: Understanding Binding Energetics in Molecular Docking
item.description:
A docking score is a balance sheet, not a binding free energy. Polar contacts have to pay back the water they displaced. A flexible ligand pays an entropy cost. A larger ligand often scores better because it makes more contacts. Read the score only after you know which of those terms the function even has.

Desolvation

Before the ligand binds, water stabilizes its polar groups and the protein surface. Binding strips some of that water. If the protein does not replace those interactions, the cost stands.

A charged amine is the example. In water it is well solvated. Buried in a hydrophobic pocket with no partner, the lost hydration shell is unfavorable even if the shape fit looks clean.

Entropy

Binding removes motion. The ligand loses translation and rotation. A flexible ligand loses conformations. Side chains at the site often order. That entropy opposes binding.

Entropy can also help. Ordered waters released into bulk solvent are more disordered than they were in the pocket. A rigid ligand pays a smaller conformational penalty than a flexible one, which is why rigidity can improve binding efficiency.

Water that was already in the pocket

Two cases:

  • A high-energy, poorly stabilized water is a good thing to displace. It gains freedom in bulk solvent.
  • A water with strong hydrogen bonds is a bad thing to displace unless the ligand restores those bonds.

Hydration analysis is how this note suggests finding the “unhappy” waters worth targeting.

Electrostatics, and the solvent around them

Salt bridges, hydrogen bonds, and dipoles are the favorable electrostatic terms. A carboxylate next to a lysine or an arginine is the example.

The same charge is stabilized by water. Bury it without a partner and the desolvation cost can exceed the interaction you gained. The electrostatic term and the desolvation term are one argument.

Larger ligands score better

More atoms make more contacts, so many scoring functions drift toward larger molecules. Ligand efficiency (LE) divides the binding energy by the number of heavy atoms. Fit quality (FQ) is the size-adjusted efficiency named alongside it. A smaller ligand with efficient contacts can be the better lead.

What each scorer actually computes

AutoDock4 is a physics-based force field. Partial charges are explicit, commonly Gasteiger-PEOE. Electrostatics are a screened Coulomb term. Hydrogen bonding and desolvation are separate terms, calibrated on experimental binding data.

Vina is an empirical function trained on experimental complexes. It does not compute partial charges and it has no classical Coulomb term. Steric fit, hydrophobic contact, and hydrogen bonds are empirical potentials. It is faster, and the electrostatics are less visible.

Smina is a Vina fork with refined empirical potentials, a torsional penalty, and a stronger hydrophobic term. It is still empirical and still does not compute partial charges.

GNINA adds a convolutional network trained on protein–ligand complexes. The network reads the 3D pattern and does not model electrostatics as a physics term. Pose prediction is the strength named here. Detailed charge effects are the gap.

Function Electrostatics Partial charges Speed Strength named here
AutoDock4 Physics-based Explicit Slower Charged systems
Vina / Smina Empirical, implicit None Fast Large screens
GNINA Neural network None Fast Pose prediction

How to read the number

The score mixes van der Waals, electrostatics, hydrogen bonds, desolvation, and some entropy-like penalties, and several of those pieces are empirical. Use it to rank compounds in one dataset. Do not read it as an absolute affinity.

Binding is the case where the contacts, the hydrophobic fit, and the release of a bad water outweigh desolvation, the frozen ligand, and the size bias in the function you chose.

item.title: Practical System Preparation Tips for Molecular Dynamics Simulations
item.description:
The trajectory is already biased before the first step. The box decides how much water you pay for. The termini decide whether a fragment carries charges it never had. The frame you pick afterwards decides whether you publish an outlier.

Which box

A cubic box is orthogonal, easy to look at, and easy to debug. For a globular protein it also packs badly: the corners fill with water that the solute never touches. That is a larger system and a higher cost for the same buffer.

A truncated octahedron is closer to a sphere. For spherical solutes it cuts the solvent count by roughly 30 to 40 percent and still wraps the solute in an even shell. It is the usual compromise.

A rhombic dodecahedron leaves the least empty solvent for a given buffer. The shape is less obvious. Current MD codes handle it. The saving matters once the solute is large. This note does not give a percent for that saving.

Box Advantage Limit
Cube Simple, and natural for an elongated solute Least efficient for a globular protein
Truncated octahedron Balance of simplicity and solvent count A less obvious geometry
Rhombic dodecahedron Smallest solvent volume Least intuitive shape

When to cap the termini

A full-length chain has a real N terminus and a real C terminus. A fragment cut out of a domain does not. The cut ends are charged as if they were the ends of the protein, and they are often buried in the parent structure. That charge invents salt bridges, pulls on the fold, and shows up later as “dynamics.”

The usual caps close the backbone. ACE is the acetyl cap on the N terminus. NME is the N-methylamide cap on the C terminus.

Cap a peptide, an isolated domain, or a stretch you extracted from a larger chain. Leave the termini alone on a full-length protein whose natural ends are solvent-exposed and part of the biology.

Which frame represents the ensemble

The frame that has wandered farthest from the start is easy to notice and a poor representative. It can be one excursion.

Pool the runs. Align on a stable reference region. Measure the variation you care about: RMSD, distances between key residues, or the pocket. Cluster. Take the centroids. Those are the conformations the ensemble actually spent time in.

item.title: Unlocking the Undruggable: How Biotechnology Is Rewriting Drug Discovery
item.description:
“Undruggable” usually means “no useful pocket for a small molecule.” KRAS, BCL-2, transcription factors, and intrinsically disordered proteins sat in that category for a long time. A few approved drugs show the label was about the modality, not about the biology being unreachable.

The figures and examples below are the ones in the DrugBank overview this note follows. They are not a new census.

How the pocket became the default

Discovery started with phenotypic screens: an extract, a phenotype. Target-based design then went after receptors, channels, and enzymes that already had a cavity. Biologics widened that, and still reached only about 2% of the human proteome. Transcription factors, flexible proteins, and broad protein–protein interfaces stayed outside.

Imatinib and the kinase inhibitors that followed are the success of the pocket strategy. They are also the demonstration of its edge.

Why the difficult targets are difficult

  • Conserved active sites make selectivity hard.
  • Intrinsically disordered proteins do not offer one binding pose.
  • Protein–protein interfaces are flat.
  • Polar, solvent-exposed surfaces fight the usual drug-like property ranges.

Venetoclax, a BCL-2 inhibitor, and sotorasib, a KRAS G12C inhibitor, are the two cases this overview uses to show that those constraints can be worked around.

Repurposing

Repurposing skips part of the early safety and manufacturing work. In the overview, it accounts for one-third of recent FDA approvals and about 25% of pharmaceutical revenue. Sildenafil, propranolol, and aspirin are the classic re-readings of an existing drug. Current practice adds transcriptomic matching, electronic health records, and network pharmacology.

The limits are the ones stated there: weaker intellectual-property protection, and data you cannot always get. The openings it names are rare disease, pandemics, and more personalized use.

Modalities that do not need a classical pocket

  • PROTACs hand the target to the cell’s degradation machinery.
  • Multispecifics, small molecules or antibodies, hit more than one function.
  • Nucleic-acid therapeutics act on expression: RNA, antisense, siRNA, gene editing.
  • Peptidomimetics copy a protein surface so they can bind a flat interface.

The same overview points at four results. Venetoclax got onto the BCL-2 interface. Sotorasib used a KRAS pocket that had not been the starting assumption. HIF-2α inhibitors reached a transcription factor. Peptilogics’ PLG0206 is the computational peptide example.

The development path is still the bottleneck

Approval rates in the 2000s are given as about 12% from Phase I to approval. The failure modes named are lack of efficacy, toxicity, and poor pharmacology. Outsourcing and academic partnerships do not remove that.

The process changes listed are adaptive trials, biomarker-based recruitment, AI-guided study planning, real-world evidence, and network pharmacology for multi-target questions. Orphan, fast-track, and breakthrough designations are the regulatory routes named alongside them.

What “druggable” is doing in this sentence

The word expands when the toolbox expands: repurposing, PROTACs, multispecifics, nucleic acids, designed peptides, high-resolution structures, and large-scale computational screening. A protein can still be a bad target. It is less often a bad target only because a small molecule cannot find a hole.

Source: DrugBank. Unlocking Undruggable Targets: Biotechnology’s Role in Expanding Drug Discovery. 2024.

item.title: How to Use DataWarrior for Drug Discovery: Key Workflows From the Villoutreix Tutorials
item.description:
DataWarrior is the triage step, not the model. Bruno Villoutreix’s tutorial series is the guided tour this note follows. Part 1 is a filter: a name pattern, then a substructure, then a row list you can export.

The practice set is the Wikipedia molecule import inside the program, on the order of 22,000 structures, depending on the version. No separate download URL is given here.

What the program is

DataWarrior is a free, open-source, chemistry-aware table. Academic and commercial use are both covered. It filters in real time on text, numbers, and structure. It draws 2D and 3D plots. It calculates properties, enumerates combinatorial libraries, runs PCA and t-SNE, and can dock into a pocket. Formats are SMILES, SDF (v2 and v3), CSV, tab-delimited text, and its own DWIR project file.

A lot of the interface is a right-click, a sub-window, or a pop-up. The useful mental model is a spreadsheet that knows what a molecule is.

Villoutreix’s series is about 85 minutes across 9 videos. Part 1 is the import-and-filter path summarized here. The videos are where the clicks are. This page does not restage them as screenshots.

The Part 1 filter

Import the Wikipedia structures from inside DataWarrior. Then:

  1. Filter names with a regular expression. The examples are .*ib for kinase inhibitors, .*sartan for angiotensin receptor blockers, and .*azole for antifungals. Applied to the Wikipedia set, each suffix is a much smaller table.
  2. Draw a fragment in the structure filter. The example is a piperazine or piperidine. Rows have to match the name rule and contain the fragment. The hit atoms are shown in red.
  3. Make a row list. The example list is named cancer. Add a SMILES column. Drop columns you do not need, such as formula, molecular weight, and the structure depiction. Save tab-delimited text, cancer.txt.

Repeat with another suffix, such as .*azole, when you want a second set.

Where it sits in a project

Bring your own SDF or SMILES in, and merge assay or ADMET columns, once the Wikipedia exercise is familiar. The same two filters apply: a name or series pattern, and a scaffold. Plots are for activity, scatter, PCA or t-SNE, and the clusters you would otherwise miss in a table. The export is the clean SMILES-plus-metadata file that docking, QSAR, molecular dynamics, or a library design step can read.

Install DataWarrior from the official site, then follow the six clicks above on the Wikipedia set before you trust the same clicks on a project table. The program is the interactive layer in front of the modeling. It is not the model.

item.title: Energy Minimization with Open Babel: Practical Guide for Ligand Preparation
item.description:
A ligand drawn by hand, or pulled from a 2D table, is often a bad start for docking. obminimize relaxes it with a small-molecule force field. It does not produce a protein-bound pose.

Downloaded or sketched ligands carry unrealistic bonds, angles, and overlaps. Docking those coordinates can bias the score or fail to converge. Minimization is the preprocessing step that makes the geometry a plausible gas-phase start. Commercial tools such as Chem3D do this too. Open Babel is the free command-line route.

The command

obminimize [options] input_file
  • -ff chooses the force field.
  • -sd is steepest descent.
  • -cg is conjugate gradient, and it is the default.
  • -h adds hydrogens.
  • -n sets the maximum number of steps. The default is 2500.
  • -o sets the output format, such as PDB, MOL2, or SDF.

Which force field

Force field Typical use Strength Weakness
GAFF General drug-like molecules AMBER-compatible Less aimed at a small ligand on its own
Ghemical Teaching, small molecules Light Limited accuracy
MMFF94 Small organic ligands Well validated A bit heavier
MMFF94s MMFF94 variant Better torsions Similar cost to MMFF94
UFF Organics, inorganics, metals Wide element coverage Weaker on ordinary organics

For a drug-like ligand, use MMFF94 or MMFF94s.

SD, then CG

Steepest descent walks the gradient. It is robust and it removes high-energy clashes. It is slow once the molecule is close to a minimum.

Conjugate gradient uses the gradient and the previous search direction. It takes fewer steps near the minimum. It can fail if the start is still far away.

So the order is SD first, CG second.

Two recorded commands

MMFF94 with steepest descent, hydrogens added, PDB out:

obminimize -sd -ff MMFF94 -h ligand.mol2 -o pdb ligand_min.pdb

UFF with conjugate gradient, for a metal complex, SDF out:

obminimize -cg -ff UFF metal_complex.mol2 -o sdf metal_min.sdf

A longer run is the same command with -n set above the default of 2500. This note does not record a specific step count, so there is no third command to copy.

The output is a ligand that is less likely to explode in docking or in the first steps of MD. It is still a force-field minimum of the free ligand, not a bound conformation and not a quantum geometry.
